lessons.title: Letter writing: formal and informal letters
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB — Anglophone primary curriculum, Level III (Classes 5 and 6), English Language — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Write an informal letter to a friend or relative.
Write a formal letter (request, apology, application) with the right layout.
Use the right opening, closing and tone.
reviewNotes: Formal letter layout (position of the date, subject line, 'Yours faithfully/sincerely') follows common Cameroonian anglophone practice; check against the FSLC marking scheme. Sample letters use fictional names.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Two kinds of letter
blocks.md: An **informal (friendly) letter** is to a friend or a relative: it can be warm and chatty. A **formal letter** is to a person in authority (the headmaster, a company, an official): it is polite, short and to the point. Use **full forms** (do not, not don't) and no slang in a formal letter.

blocks.caption: The layout of a formal letter.
blocks.alt: A page showing a formal letter: the sender's address and the date at the top right, the receiver's name and address at the left, Dear Sir, a subject line, the body, Yours faithfully and the sender's name.

blocks.title: Layout of a formal letter
blocks.md:
1. Your address (top right), then the date.
2. The name and address of the person you write to (left).
3. **Dear Sir / Madam,** (or **Dear Mr Ndi,**).
4. A **subject line** in capital letters.
5. The body: why you write, the details, what you ask for, thanks.
6. **Yours faithfully,** (if you wrote Dear Sir/Madam) or **Yours sincerely,** (if you wrote the person's name), then your name.

blocks.title: Informal letter
blocks.md: Address and date at the top right, then **Dear Ada,** and a friendly first line (*I hope you are well.*). Write about the news, ask questions, then close with *Your friend,* or *Yours lovingly,* and your first name. There is no subject line and no receiver's address.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Mixing the endings: *Dear Sir ... Yours sincerely* (should be faithfully).
- Using slang, short forms or a long story in a formal letter.
- Forgetting the date, the subject line or your name.
- Writing the whole letter in one paragraph.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Which closing do you use after Dear Sir and after Dear Mr Ndi?
steps: Dear Sir (the name is not known): Yours faithfully.
Dear Mr Ndi (the name is known): Yours sincerely.
blocks.answer: Dear Sir ... Yours faithfully; Dear Mr Ndi ... Yours sincerely.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Write the first two sentences of a formal letter to your headmaster asking permission to be absent for one day.
steps: Start with the reason and the request: I am writing to ask for your permission to be absent from school on Friday, 10 May.
Give the reason politely: I have to attend my cousin's wedding in Bafoussam. I thank you in advance.
blocks.answer: I am writing to ask for your permission to be absent from school on Friday. I have to attend a family wedding in Bafoussam.

lessons.title: Writing a story and describing a person, place or event
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB — Anglophone primary curriculum, Level III (Classes 5 and 6), English Language — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Plan a story with a beginning, a problem, a climax and an ending.
Use the past tense, paragraphs and linking words in a story.
Use the five senses and good adjectives in a description.
reviewNotes: Marking schemes for compositions are examples only; the FSLC scheme and expected length should be checked.
Sample answers are original and should be proof-read.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Planning a story
blocks.md: Before you write, make a short plan: **who** (characters), **where and when** (setting), **what happens** (the problem), **how it ends**. Use one paragraph for each part. Write in the **past tense** and use linking words: first, then, suddenly, after that, at last.

blocks.caption: The shape of a story.
blocks.alt: A line goes up like a mountain. The points are marked Beginning, Problem, Climax at the top, Solution and Ending.

blocks.title: Writing a description
blocks.md: To describe a place, a person or an event, use your **five senses**: what you see, hear, smell, taste and feel. Use exact adjectives (*a crowded, noisy market*) and comparisons (*as busy as ants*). Describe in order (from left to right, near to far) so that the reader can picture the scene.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Starting to write without a plan, so that the story has no clear ending.
- Changing from past to present tense in the middle of the story.
- Using the same word again and again (*nice*, *good*): choose a more exact word.
- Writing a long list of events with no paragraphs.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Plan a story called 'The Lost Bag'.
steps: Beginning: Neba goes to the market with her mother and carries her new school bag.
Problem and climax: she puts the bag down and it disappears; she searches and cries.
Solution and ending: a kind seller found it; Neba thanks him and promises to be careful.
blocks.answer: A plan with a beginning, a problem, a climax and an ending.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Improve this sentence with a description: The dog was big.
steps: Add adjectives that show what you see: huge, brown.
Add an action and a sound: barked loudly at the gate.
Together: The huge brown dog barked loudly at the gate.
blocks.answer: The huge brown dog barked loudly at the gate.

objectives: Find rhyming words and the rhyme scheme of a poem.
Name the parts of a poem: line, stanza, rhythm.
reviewNotes: The poem is an original four-line poem written for this lesson. Metaphor is introduced only briefly; check the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Parts of a poem
blocks.md: A poem is written in **lines**. A group of lines is a **stanza** (verse). **Rhyme** is when words end with the same sound: night / light, song / long. **Rhythm** is the beat of the words when we read aloud. The **rhyme scheme** is the pattern of rhymes: we give the same letter to lines that rhyme (A A B B or A B A B).

items.text: When rain drums on our roof at night,
The street lamps glow with silver light.
The frogs sing out a happy song,
And croak the whole night long.
night / light rhyme (A).  song / long rhyme (B).

blocks.caption: A four-line poem with the rhyme scheme A A B B.
blocks.alt: The four lines of a poem. The first two lines end with night and light and are marked A. The last two end with song and long and are marked B.

blocks.title: Poetry words
blocks.md: A **simile** compares two things with *like* or *as*: *as brave as a lion*. A **metaphor** says that one thing is another: *the moon is a silver coin*. **Alliteration** repeats the first sound: *Peter picked ripe red plums*. **Repetition** repeats a word or line for effect. To understand a poem: read it aloud, find the topic, find the feeling, and look at the pictures the words make in your mind.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking that rhyming words must be **spelled** alike: they must **sound** alike (light / write).
- Answering a poem question with a long story: say what the poem is about and how it makes you feel, in your own words.
- Mixing up simile (like/as) and metaphor (no like/as).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Find the rhyming words in: The frogs sing out a happy song, and croak the whole night long.
steps: Look at the last word of each line: song and long.
They end with the same sound -ong, so they rhyme.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Complete the simile: as brave as a ......
steps: A simile compares two things with as ... as.
A lion is a common sign of courage, so: as brave as a lion.

lessons.title: Oral English and dictation: sounds, syllables, stress and listening
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB — Anglophone primary curriculum, Level III (Classes 5 and 6), English Language — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Count the syllables in a word and find the stressed syllable.
Pronounce and spell common difficult words, including silent letters.
Use polite expressions and prepare a short oral talk; write a dictation correctly.
reviewNotes: Syllable counts and stress patterns are for British English; the audio block is read by the device text-to-speech voice, so its pronunciation (accent) is not controlled. Dictation of the audio sentence should be checked by a teacher.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Syllables and stress
blocks.md: A **syllable** is a beat in a word that has one vowel sound: *pen* (1), *man-go* (2), *ba-na-na* (3), *beau-ti-ful* (3). In words of more than one syllable, one syllable is **stressed**: said louder and longer. *Teacher* is TEA-cher; *Cameroon* is Cam-er-OON; *banana* is ba-NA-na.

blocks.caption: Syllables are the beats of a word.
blocks.alt: Boxes showing syllables. Banana has three boxes: ba, na and na. Mango has two boxes: man and go. Text says where the stress falls.

blocks.title: Silent letters and sounds
blocks.md: Some letters are written but not said: **k** in *knife* and *know*; **w** in *write* and *answer*; **b** in *lamb* and *climb*; **h** in *hour* and *honest*; **gh** in *night* and *daughter*. Learn the commonly confused sounds in a list: ship / sheep, bit / beat, pull / pool.

blocks.title: Dictation and speaking
blocks.md: **Dictation**: listen to the whole sentence first, then write it while it is read in small pieces, then listen again and check spelling and punctuation. **Speaking**: greet politely (*Good morning, madam.*), ask politely (*May I come in, please?*), look at your listener, speak clearly and not too fast. For a short talk: introduction, two or three points, conclusion.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing a word the way it sounds (*nife*, *rite*): check the silent letters.
- Counting letters instead of **syllables**.
- Forgetting capital letters and full stops in a dictation.
- Speaking too fast, so that the listener cannot follow.

blocks.text: Listen and write. The children walked to school in the morning. They were happy, because the teacher had promised a story.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: How many syllables are in 'beautiful'? Where is the stress?
steps: Split into beats: beau-ti-ful: three syllables.
The first syllable is said louder: BEAU-ti-ful.
blocks.answer: Three syllables; stress on the first: BEAU-ti-ful.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Which letters are silent in 'knife' and 'lamb'?
steps: In knife the k is not pronounced: we say 'nife'.
In lamb the b is silent: we say 'lam'.
blocks.answer: k in knife; b in lamb.

exercises.prompt: Write a story of about 10 to 12 sentences with the title 'A Surprise on the Way to School'. Use the past tense and give your story a beginning, a problem and an ending.
exercises.model: Last Monday I left home early to go to school. I walked along the dusty road and sang a song. Suddenly I heard a small cry from the bushes.
